newsitem.title: FRANCE: Sleaze, far right dominate French vote debate.
newsitem.headline: Sleaze, far right dominate French vote debate.

text.p: France's politicians traded charges about sleaze and of secret complicity with the extreme right anti-immigrant National Front on Friday as campaigning for a parliamentary election cut with a new edge of nastiness.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe, whose centre-right coalition has a clear lead in opinion polls, dismissed charges that he was secretly preparing an amnesty to pardon political sleaze if his coalition wins the May 25-June 1 vote.
"It's pure fabrication," he told the daily Le Parisien. "There, as in other cases, justice will be done."
The opposition says the election was brought forward almost 10 months partly to stifle burgeoning cases of political corruption.

Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin turned the focus onto sleaze by branding Paris the "capital of opaqueness" in an attack targeting conservative President Jacques Chirac, who was mayor from 1977 to 1995, when he won the presidency.

"Corruption, scandals, networks of secret funding, cynical policies towards the poor and the young: Paris...has become the exclusive property of a few since 1997," he said in a late-night rally on Thursday.
Juppe said disputes over funding of political parties were "a true problem from which we will not escape for a long time." On Thursday, he accused the opposition of "wicked and vicious soundbites".

Charges of illicit funding of most political parties through rake-offs on public contracts, including in Paris, have plagued France for years. An amnesty voted in 1990 by a parliament dominated by the left sparked a furious row.

Junior Minister for Urban Affairs Eric Raoult kept up taunting the Socialists after National Front party leader Jean-Marie Le Pen said he would prefer a victory by the left than the right, reckoning it would undermine Chirac.
"I fear that Lionel Jospin does not like the ideas of Mr Le Pen on the hustings but that he's wild about Mr Le Pen's votes in the ballot box," Raoult told Europe 1 radio.

Le Pen said on Thursday that he reckoned a left-wing victory could derail Chirac's plans to take France into the euro single currency that would lead to a Europe which, Le Pen said, would make "Hitler's dream come true".

Jospin, who has toned down Socialist enthusiasm for the euro during the campaign, fiercely denounced the ruling coalition for portraying him as a tacit ally of Le Pen, a bitter opponent of the Maastricht Treaty.

"If there is any leakage, it is between the ideas of the far-right and the right, never with the left's ideas," he said. Le Pen's party, which openly espouses racial inequality, carries some 15 percent of the electorate.

A senior Front politician and member of the European Parliament, Bernard Antony, was given a six-month suspended prison sentence and fined 50,000 francs ($8,800) on Friday for making racial insults towards Africans.

The Paris stock market, partly encouraged polls showing the right was set to retain power, rose to a new all-time high on Friday in the wake of Wall Street gains. The CAC-40 index was up 0.9 percent at 2,801 in early afternoon.
The latest opinion poll, by Ipsos, said the centre-right would retain a clear majority with 323 seats -- up from 290 a week ago -- to the combined left's 253. The National Front would get one.
